title: Quantization technical review - Equinox AI

Agreed to run controlled benchmarks (GPTQ vs AWQ) on Equinox model shard with 8k context and KV-cache heavy traces; Redwood to provide benchmark script, configuration suggestions, and draft SLO guidance.

transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. uh quick intros — Jordan from Redwood AE, Sanaya our SE focusing on inference, Liam on the solutions side.
[00:14] Priya Raman: Hi, this is Priya, CTO at Equinox. We have Miguel, Alex and Ravi on the line.
[00:22] Miguel Santos: Morning. We're trying to understand quantization tradeoffs for our 13B transformer model, primarily latency and accuracy regressions we've observed in INT8.
[00:35] Sanaya Gupta: Great. The agenda: we'll walk through INT8/FP8, then GPTQ/AWQ practicals, runtime impacts like KV cache and batching, and VPC/on-prem notes.
[00:50] Alex Chen: Quick context — infra is VPC-hosted, multi-tenant, we want deterministic p99 latency under 350ms for 2k token contexts. Also pref the option to move to on-prem if needed for residency.
[01:07] Liam O'Connor: Noted. When you say deterministic, is that cold-start plus generation or steady-state?
[01:15] Ravi Patel: Steady-state, but tail spikes during long prefix KV cache misses.
[01:22] Sanaya Gupta: OK. So first, quantization modes: INT8 gives big memory and throughput wins but sometimes causes accuracy drift on narrow layers, FP8 tends to keep accuracy but needs hardware that supports FP8 kernels. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training quant methods — GPTQ preserves range better in many cases, AWQ is faster to run but you'll see some layer-specific variance.
[01:45] Miguel Santos: We've tried INT8 with GPTQ and still saw regressions on some instruction-following tasks, outputs were more hallucination-prone.
[01:53] Sanaya Gupta: That's common, yeah. A couple of mitigation patterns: per-channel quantization on attention projection weights, selective quantization (leave layernorm/final lm head in fp16), or using AWQ with calibration on a representative prompt set.
[02:10] Priya Raman: Can you explain AWQ vs GPTQ in runtime terms? Which is lower latency?
[02:17] Sanaya Gupta: AWQ tends to produce smaller kernels in some runtimes and can be faster at generation time — but it depends on kernel fusion and the backend. GPTQ often yields slightly better quality but larger memory footprint for the corrected scales. On our runtime (Redwood serving) we see AWQ infer slightly faster on A100/80GB in many cases, but GPTQ is more robust on instruction tasks.
[02:41] Jordan Park: We can share numbers — our internal benchmark sheet that compares p50/p95/p99 latency with 2k context, batched vs single, and KV cache warm/cold.
[02:51] Alex Chen: That would help. Also, about KV cache, we see big jumps when cache misses require recomputing prefix. How does Redwood handle prefix/KV caching and sharding?
[03:02] Sanaya Gupta: Redwood uses prefix KV caching with LRU eviction by default and persistent per-session cache when possible. For multi-tenant you can set cache isolation policies or per-customer namespaces. We also have a warm-cache option where you seed the cache for anticipated prefixes. Note — in quantized models, KV cache representations can be smaller but you might see precision loss if you aggressively quantize the cache entries.
[03:26] Miguel Santos: Hmm, by precision loss do you mean more divergence over long contexts?
[03:30] Sanaya Gupta: Exactly. Small rounding errors accumulate across long autoregressive steps, so for 8k contexts we've seen minor drift in topic coherence when using INT8 fully end-to-end. That's why selective FP16 for KV or using higher-precision cache storage is sometimes recommended.
[03:46] Priya Raman: If we do a hybrid — store KV in FP16 but weights in INT8 — what's the runtime hit?
[03:52] Liam O'Connor: There's a modest memory increase for cache but compute stays faster because the matmuls use INT8 kernels. On our benchmarks p95 latency increased ~8-12ms vs fully INT8 but accuracy improved noticeably.
[04:06] Ravi Patel: Are there known pitfalls with batching? Our traffic is bursty; we want to tune batching window to avoid p99 spikes.
[04:12] Sanaya Gupta: Right. Continuous batching benefits throughput, but increases latency if you hold too long. Redwood supports adaptive batching: a max wait time + max batch size. For KV-heavy requests, batching can actually reduce total compute per token due to shared KV reads, but increases scheduling jitter. For your p99 target we usually recommend small max wait (3-5ms) and conservative batch size (4-8) for 13B models.
[04:38] Miguel Santos: On quantization-induced hallucinations — any calibration best practices?
[04:44] Sanaya Gupta: Use representative prompts for calibration, include instruction-style and few-shot variants. Run a small eval set (1k examples) after quantization and compute quality deltas; if regression > threshold (you pick, e.g., BLEU/EM/ROUGE or custom fidelity), do selective layer exclusion. Also consider activation outlier handling — clamp or per-channel scales.
[05:07] Priya Raman: We're also considering FP8 in future hardware upgrades. Is FP8 significantly better quality-wise than INT8?
[05:15] Sanaya Gupta: FP8 can be closer to FP16 in many cases, especially for attention softmax and layernorm internals. The caveat is hardware support — some clouds support FP8 on newer amps but portability is lower. If you can standardize on HW that supports FP8, it's a good middle ground for preserving quality and getting memory savings.
[05:33] Alex Chen: For our on-prem path, what are the Redwood private constraints? Does private support same optimized kernels?
[05:40] Jordan Park: Yes — Redwood Private ships the same runtime; some optimized proprietary kernels require compatible CUDA/toolkit versions. We'll produce a compatibility matrix. For on-prem we also offer assistance with kernel builds and recommended container specs.
[05:55] Miguel Santos: Any tips for deterministic p99 when moving from hosted to private? We're worried about noisy neighbors and infra jitter.
[06:02] Liam O'Connor: For private we recommend dedicating GPU pools (reservation) or using cgroup limits for CPU/IO; pin interrupts and use isolated NUMA configs. Redwood Dedicated offers reserved capacity with SLA that mirrors that setup if you want to avoid building ops.
[06:18] Sanaya Gupta: Also, measure end-to-end with real traces — which Alex will upload — because synthetic microbenchmarks miss prefix-heavy behaviors.
[06:27] Alex Chen: We'll do that.
[06:29] Priya Raman: Back to benchmarks: can Redwood share a reproducible script? We prefer something we can run in CI against each quant build.
[06:36] Jordan Park: Yes — we'll share a bench repo + quickstart with container image, the GPTQ/AWQ conversion steps, and an eval harness that computes fidelity metrics.
[06:45] Miguel Santos: Great. Timeline?
[06:48] Jordan Park: We'll send the scripts this week, you upload traces by Nov 8, we'll run a Redwood-hosted baseline and a GPTQ/AWQ run and reconvene the week of Nov 16.
[06:58] Ravi Patel: One more ask — security: what about KMS integration for private?
[07:02] Sanaya Gupta: Private supports KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs for model access are available. We'll attach our SOC2 docs and a short architecture note.
[07:12] Priya Raman: Perfect.
[07:15] Liam O'Connor: quick note — on the benchmarking sheet we'll surface p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, memory footprint, and an accuracy delta column so you can correlate latency gains to accuracy loss.
[07:27] Miguel Santos: Useful.
[07:29] Jordan Park: Any other questions?
[07:32] Priya Raman: Not at the moment, thanks.
[07:34] Jordan Park: Ok recap: Jordan to send scripts and bench sheet, Sanaya to propose quant profiles, Alex to provide traces, meet week of Nov 16 to review.
[07:44] Miguel Santos: Thank you all.
[07:46] Jordan Park: Thanks, bye.
